Article Title: Owaisi-Azad alliance looks strong on paper, but Akhilesh Yadav has little to fear: 5 reasons why SP may not be worried
Article Text:
The battle for UP

I am ready to join hands. I am ready to form an alliance. Today is the time to talk. Don't cry later after the elections are over. We don't want the BJP to come to power again. Asaduddin Owaisi, AIMIM

An additional option will now be available to such innocent people who cast their votes after being misled. This will cause the BJP a loss of 2-3 per cent votes. The BJP will be left with nothing. Samajwadi Party chief, Akhilesh Yadav

Akhilesh has worked hard to change the SP's pro-Muslim image

The SP increased its tally from 17 seats in 2017 to 34 in 2022, while the BJP's count fell from 39 to 22 across 59 constituencies.

Azad's primary battle is with Mayawati

Owaisi's success in Bihar is no guarantee of success in UP

Owaisi's party won five seats in Bihar in both 2020 and 2025, but failed to win a single seat in Uttar Pradesh in 2017 and 2022.

An alliance born out of limited choices

Samajwadi Party remains the strongest challenger to the BJP

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

When Asaduddin Owaisi and Chandrashekhar Azad joined hands on November 12, the immediate question was whether the alliance of AIMIM and Azad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram) would become Akhilesh Yadav 's biggest worry ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections.After all, the two communities they are seeking to mobilise, Muslims and Dalits, are key to Akhilesh's PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak backward classes, Dalits and minorities) formula, which helped the Samajwadi Party (SP) emerge as the single-largest party in UP in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections.Owaisi had been reaching out to Akhilesh for an alliance since July, even warning him not to regret rejecting the offer if the BJP returned to power. Interestingly, Owaisi was targeting the SP more than the BJP in his election meetings.Four months later, with his attempts to forge an alliance with the SP and BSP chief Mayawati yielding no results, Owaisi joined hands with Azad to form the Samajik Parivartan Morcha.Akhilesh, however, appears unfazed. He claimed the new front would cost the BJP, rather than his party, 2-3% of its votes. He also ruled out expanding the SP's existing alliance.So, is Akhilesh right in playing down the threat? Here are five reasons why the Owaisi-Azad alliance may not be as big a worry as it appears.Akhilesh Yadav has made a conscious effort to move away from the image of Muslim appeasement that the Samajwadi Party acquired under his father Mulayam Singh Yadav.While Mulayam openly flaunted Muslim voters and built his party's electoral strength around the Muslim-Yadav combination, Akhilesh has been trying to expand the SP's appeal among Hindu voters without alienating its traditional support base.From visiting temples and attending Durga Puja celebrations to hosting iftar gatherings, Akhilesh has been trying to strike a balance between the two communities.The change became particularly evident after the BJP's sweeping victory in the 2017 assembly elections, when the SP began making Akhilesh's religious engagements more public.Since then, Akhilesh has visited the Vindhyachal temple in Mirzapur and the Ravidas temple in Varanasi, installed a 51-foot statue of Lord Krishna in Saifai and initiated the construction of the Kedareshwar temple in Etawah.On December 12, Akhilesh and his wife Dimple Yadav are scheduled to make their first visit to the Ram Temple in Ayodhya since its consecration in January 2024.At the same time, his outreach to Muslims has continued. However, Akhilesh has been careful to avoid giving the BJP an opportunity to accuse the SP of Muslim appeasement.Joining hands with Owaisi could undo some of that work and give the BJP fresh ammunition against the SP. By rejecting an alliance with AIMIM, Akhilesh may actually be helping himself retain the broader support base he has built over the years.Chandrashekhar Azad is a leader known for taking aggressive political positions that keeps him in the news. But in Uttar Pradesh, he faces a tough challenge from Mayawati, who continues to command the support of a significant section of Dalit voters.Azad's victory from Nagina in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections established him as a Dalit leader to watch. He defeated the BJP candidate by over 1.5 lakh votes, while the SP finished a distant third and the BSP fourth.However, one Lok Sabha victory does not establish Azad as a leader of Dalits across UP. In the 2022 assembly elections, he contested against Yogi Adityanath from Gorakhpur Urban, secured fewer than 8,000 votes and lost his deposit."Jatavs, who account for around 11% of Uttar Pradesh's population, are still largely loyal to Mayawati. In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, non-Jatav Dalits, particularly the Pasis, shifted towards the INDIA bloc. This played an important role in the alliance's performance," said Pravin Kumar, senior political observer and Resident Editor of TOI, Lucknow.According to the CSDS-Lokniti post-poll survey, 44% of Jatav voters in UP backed the BSP in 2024, even though the party failed to win a single Lok Sabha seat.Moreover, Mayawati has brought her nephew Akash Anand back into the party and reinstated him as national convener, tasking him with expanding the BSP's appeal among young voters.Interestingly, when Mayawati removed Anand from the party in September, Azad had invited him to join the Azad Samaj Party.While Azad enjoys popularity among sections of Dalit youth, his ability to turn that popularity into votes across the state is yet to be established.AIMIM won five assembly seats each in Bihar in 2020 and 2025. However, Owaisi has struggled to make a similar impact in Uttar Pradesh."Owaisi has not been able to replicate his success in Bihar in Uttar Pradesh. The only time AIMIM made its presence felt was during the 2023 urban local body elections, when it won five chairperson seats and around 75 councillor seats. But these were just flashes of success, not signs of a larger political shift," Pravin Kumar said.In Bihar, Owaisi found a strong base in Seemanchal, a region with a large concentration of Muslim voters. All five seats won by AIMIM in both elections came from this region.In UP, however, AIMIM failed to win a single seat despite contesting 38 constituencies in 2017 and 95 in 2022. Its vote share in the last assembly elections was less than 1%.While Muslims account for around 19% of UP's population, their presence is spread across several regions. Owaisi is yet to establish a stronghold comparable to Seemanchal, while the SP enjoys considerable support among Muslim voters.Despite nearly a decade of contesting elections in UP, AIMIM is still looking for its first assembly seat.Chandrashekhar Azad was not Owaisi's first choice for an alliance in Uttar Pradesh. The AIMIM chief had repeatedly approached Akhilesh Yadav to join hands against the BJP.When the SP showed no interest, AIMIM reached out to Mayawati's Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), hoping to bring Muslims and Dalits together. However, that attempt also failed, and Owaisi eventually joined hands with Azad.But forming an alliance is one thing and getting voters to support each other's candidates is another.While Azad enjoys support among sections of Dalit youth, his ability to mobilise Dalits across the state and transfer their votes to AIMIM candidates is yet to be tested.Similarly, Owaisi will have to convince Muslim voters to back candidates fielded by Azad's party instead of the SP. For now, both Owaisi and Azad have far more to prove in the upcoming assembly elections than Akhilesh.In Uttar Pradesh, Muslim voters have largely backed parties they believe are best placed to defeat the BJP. For now, that party is the Samajwadi Party, not AIMIM.According to the CSDS-Lokniti post-poll survey, around 79% of Muslim voters backed the SP-led alliance in the 2022 assembly elections. In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, 92% backed the SP-Congress alliance.The alliance won 43 of UP's 80 Lok Sabha seats, with the SP alone winning 37, compared to the BJP's 33.Akhilesh's position is also reflected in his ongoing seat-sharing negotiations with the Congress. Though the arrangement is yet to be finalised, he has made it clear that seats will be allocated based on each party's chances of winning them.While Owaisi is asking Muslims to move away from traditional political parties and build their own leadership, Akhilesh is offering them an alliance that has already demonstrated its ability to defeat the BJP.And as long as defeating the BJP remains a priority for a large section of Muslim voters in UP, convincing them to shift their support away from the SP may not be easy for Owaisi.On paper, the Owaisi-Azad alliance looks promising, with Muslims and Dalits together accounting for around 40% of UP's population. But the reality on the ground is different. Owaisi has struggled to replicate his Bihar success, while Azad is yet to establish statewide appeal. The alliance could influence closely contested seats, particularly in western UP, where Owaisi has some support.So, while the alliance may appear to be a threat to Akhilesh's PDA formula on paper, both leaders have several electoral challenges of their own to overcome.And that is perhaps why Akhilesh has little reason to be worried, at least for now.
Article Summary: Akhilesh Yadav has made a conscious effort to move away from the image of Muslim appeasement that the Samajwadi Party acquired under his father Mulayam Singh Yadav. He has been trying to expand the SP's appeal among Hindu voters without alienating its traditional support base.

Why Siraj's exclusion has raised eyebrows

NEW DELHI: The selection of India's playing XI has triggered a face-off between the Congress and the BJP, with the opposition alleging discrimination against pacer Mohammed Siraj and the ruling party accusing it of dragging communal politics into cricket.The exchange began after India’s team management opted for a four-pronged pace attack but left out Siraj against New Zealand, despite the Hyderabad pacer’s impressive record and reputation for delivering in challenging conditions.Congress MP Imran Masood questioned Siraj’s exclusion, suggesting that his religious identity could have played a role in the decision."His name is Siraj -- isn't that reason enough? If he is performing and still not getting selected, what else could be the reason behind it? This alone can be the reason; there can be no other reason besides this," Masood told news agency IANS.In another interaction, the Congress MP said it was being pointed out that Siraj had performed well but was still not included in the team. "If you are not selecting him despite his good performance, the discrimination is clear," he told news agency ANI.The BJP was quick to hit back, accusing the Congress of turning team selection into a communal issue and using cricket for vote-bank politics.BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said, "Shame on Congress! Congress now does vote bank politics even in Cricket team selection! Congress says - 'Siraj was left out because he was a Muslim'."Pointing out that all-rounder Ravindra Jadeja had also been left out, Bhandari said, "Every cricketer wears the jersey representing India! Stop dividing Indian cricket team for vote bank and communal politics!"Siraj's omission has also drawn attention because of the role he has played in India's pace attack over the past few years.Fifteen months ago, on a cloudy morning in London, Siraj stepped out of Jasprit Bumrah's shadow to produce one of the most memorable performances of his career. The pacer emptied the tank on the final day of a gruelling five-Test series to help India secure a 2-2 draw against England at The Oval.His performance appeared to signal the beginning of a new phase in his career, with Siraj emerging as a potential leader of India's pace attack as Bumrah entered an intensive workload management programme.However, the pacer was left out on Thursday despite conditions in Wellington appearing tailor-made for seam bowling. The team management instead went ahead with four other seamers.One possible reason for the decision could be Siraj's recent form. His underwhelming performance against Sri Lanka in the Colombo Test three months ago may have prompted the team management to reassess his place in the playing XI.
Article Summary: Mohammed Siraj left out of India's pace attack against New Zealand. Congress alleges discrimination, BJP says stop dividing team for vote bank and communal politics. India's team management opted for a four-pronged pace attack but left out Siraj.

Article Title: Pahalgam attack: Beijing yet to share info on how GoPro camera US supplied to China was found on terrorists
Article Text:
Security personnel rushed to the spot after terrorists attacked a group of tourists at Pahalgam on April 22. (PTI)

Chinese-origin weapons also under investigation

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: China is yet to respond to India's request for information on a US-made GoPro camera recovered from the terrorists involved in the 2025 Pahalgam massacre, NIA director general Rakesh Aggarwal said on Friday. He added that investigators had gathered some forensic evidence in the case."We have not received any reply so far… But we have some forensic evidence," Aggarwal told reporters when asked whether Beijing had responded to the agency's communication about the device.The camera has become a key lead in the NIA's efforts to trace the cross-border supply networks that provide equipment to Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT). During the investigation, the agency approached US manufacturer GoPro Inc to establish the device's sales history. The company informed investigators that the camera had originally been shipped to an authorised commercial distributor in China, officials said.Investigators are now trying to establish how it moved from the Chinese distributor into the hands of LeT operatives. Officials are examining the possibility that the devices were procured by the Pakistan Army and subsequently supplied to terrorist groups, although this remains under investigation.India does not have a Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT) with China, meaning requests for information in such cases are pursued through diplomatic channels.The camera was recovered from the terrorists killed in an encounter in the Dachigam forests in July 2025, months after the attack on tourists in Pahalgam's Baisaran meadows. Investigators believe terrorist groups in Jammu and Kashmir have increasingly used body-worn and tactical cameras to record attacks for propaganda and psychological warfare.The camera is not the only piece of equipment that has drawn investigators' attention to China. Officials said at least two AK-47 rifles recovered from the Baisaran attack site and another recovered from the Dachigam encounter site were also of Chinese origin.The three terrorists involved in the massacre are believed to have escaped through the Pahalgam jungles after the attack on April 22, 2025, possibly using a vehicle. Investigators believe they had a window of nearly 40 minutes before security forces could fully assess the scale of the attack.A vehicle bearing a Shopian registration number was spotted on a road leading out of Pahalgam, but investigators lost track of it after finding that several CCTV cameras along the route were not functioning.The NIA has filed a chargesheet against LeT and six individuals, including the three slain terrorists – Faisal Jatt alias Suleman, Habeeb Tahir alias Chottu and Hamza Afghani – as well as the outfit's self-styled commander Sajid Jatt alias Sajid Jutt. Two local residents, Bashir Ahmad Jothatd and Parvaiz Ahmad, were also named for allegedly providing food and shelter to the terrorists before the attack.Two local residents, Bashir Ahmad Jothatd and Parvaiz Ahmad, have also been named for allegedly providing food and shelter to the terrorists in the days before the attack. Investigators said the men had supplied them with provisions, including turmeric, red chillies and salt, as well as cooking utensils, blankets and a tarpaulin.A blanket recovered from the Dachigam encounter site was traced to Bashir's home, officials said. A hair strand found on it was matched through DNA testing to the blanket taken from his house on April 21, 2025.On April 22, 2025, terrorists killed 26 people, mostly tourists, in the Baisaran meadows of Pahalgam. The massacre prompted India to launch Operation Sindoor, targeting terror infrastructure in Pakistan-controlled territories, including camps belonging to the banned LeT and Jaish-e-Mohammed.The three attackers were later killed by Army special forces in an encounter in the Dachigam forests on the outskirts of Srinagar.
Article Summary: China is yet to respond to India's request for information on a US-made GoPro camera recovered from the terrorists involved in the 2025 Pahalgam massacre. The camera has become a key lead in the NIA's efforts to trace the cross-border supply networks that provide equipment to Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba.

Article Title: No brakes required: How India's highways are now charging toll without stopping you
Article Text:
Inside India’s biggest toll overhaul since FASTag

How the system works

Six months, seven plazas

What happens when the payment fails

The early numbers

What the government expects to save

The plan for the next phase

Passes for the frequent traveller

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The risks that remain

The road ahead

For two decades the toll plaza has been a fixture of the Indian highway: the slowing down, the queue, the wait for a barrier to lift. Over the past six months, at a handful of locations across the country, that routine has started to disappear. Vehicles now pass under overhead gantries without stopping, and the toll is settled electronically afterwards.The technology is called Multi-Lane Free Flow, or MLFF. It lets vehicles pass through toll locations without stopping. It is still a small part of a very large network, but it marks the biggest change in how India collects highway tolls since FASTag made cashless payment routine.MLFF does not replace FASTag. It builds on it. The framework combines Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) with FASTag-based electronic collection: cameras read number plates as vehicles pass under gantries, and the FASTag account is debited automatically. Because of the “One Vehicle, One Tag” policy, each FASTag is tied to a vehicle’s registration number, so the equipment can create a toll transaction by reading the tag, the number plate, or both.The government says the aim is a faster and cleaner journey. NHAI says the technology should cut travel time, improve fuel efficiency, and make road transport safer and more sustainable.The first site went live on 1 May 2026. NHAI announced India’s first MLFF system at the Chorayasi Toll Plaza on the Surat–Bharuch section of NH-48 in Gujarat.Mundka-Bakkarwala on the Urban Extension Road-II in the Delhi-NCR region followed as the second. Union Minister Nitin Gadkari inaugurated it.The summer brought more. Rajasthan’s first MLFF plaza opened at Daulatpura on the Delhi–Jaipur section of NH-48 on 19 June. Gharaunda on the Panipat–Jalandhar section of NH-44 came next, and Manoharpura on the Delhi–Jaipur road followed on 1 July. Shahjahanpur, also on NH-48 in Rajasthan, went live in August. With that, all three plazas on the corridor supported non-stop passage. The system then moved south. On 1 October, NHAI rolled out Tamil Nadu’s first MLFF system at Paranur Toll Plaza on the Tambaram–Tindivanam section of NH-179B. Seven plazas are now operational.That is slower than planned. NHAI had targeted 17 plazas across nine states by September 2026.The harder question is what happens when the FASTag does not work. Without a booth, there is no one to stop the vehicle. The framework answers this with an electronic notice, or e-notice.If the FASTag balance is insufficient, or the tag is invalid or non-functional, the motorist is issued an e-notice and must pay the normal fee within 72 hours. After that, the amount is charged at twice the normal rate for the vehicle category. The notice is sent by SMS to the mobile number registered against the vehicle in the VAHAN database, and to the number linked to the FASTag. The mechanism rests on Rule 14 of the National Highway Fee Rules, 2008.Notices can be checked and paid on the designated portal, and a grievance can be raised there within the same 72 hours. The e-notice can also be viewed on the Rajmargyatra mobile app. The stakes of ignoring one go beyond the doubled fee. Non-payment may lead to the FASTag being blacklisted and to restrictions on other vehicle-related services through the VAHAN platform.multi lane free flow mlff barrierless tolling what to know features how to check enoticeNHAI’s advice to motorists is plain. Keep the FASTag balance sufficient, keep the tag active and properly affixed on the windshield, and use a clear High Security Registration Plate, whose laser-etched serial number the ANPR cameras can read.A Crisil Intelligence analysis gives the first real measure of how the system is performing. By 1 August, six plazas had together processed more than 110 lakh vehicle transactions and collected over Rs 147 crore in toll revenue since Choryasi opened. Choryasi led on revenue at more than Rs 51 crore, while Mundka handled the highest volume, at over 41.5 lakh transactions.FASTag is still doing most of the work. It accounted for roughly 94 per cent of revenue between May and July, about Rs 138.4 crore, against Rs 9.2 crore collected through e-notices. The notice figures show how large the compliance problem is. About 10 per cent of vehicles passing through the operational plazas triggered a payment failure, roughly 10.5 lakh notices in all.The ministry’s case rests on money, fuel and emissions. It expects MLFF to cut operational costs by Rs 5,000–6,000 crore a year and save around 250 crore litres of fuel annually, which it puts at nearly 81,000 tonnes less CO2, mainly by reducing idling and congestion at toll points. Once fully rolled out, the system is projected to handle more than 450 crore vehicle passages a year.The current network is a pilot compared with what is planned. NHAI has invited bids to extend MLFF to 104 more plazas across Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Gujarat and Rajasthan. Combined with plazas already operational or awarded, that would bring the total to 121. That is only 10–11 per cent of the more than 1,150 physical plazas now active nationwide.The shift comes alongside changes to how regular users pay. The annual FASTag pass, launched in August 2025, was being used by around 52 per cent of private vehicles at these plazas. Its standard price is Rs 3,075.A cheaper option for people who live near plazas took effect on 1 November. The ministry introduced a Concessional Local Pass for eligible non-commercial vehicle owners living within 20 km of a fee plaza. It costs Rs 1,500 a year at plazas outside municipal or local town limits and Rs 3,000 at those within them. Eligible owners with a valid, working FASTag can choose between this and the existing monthly pass. The pass is valid only at the plaza for which it is issued and cannot be transferred.Officials expect it to encourage more commuters to link their vehicles to FASTag, and so reduce e-notices.The Crisil analysis lists the system’s weak points. It points to revenue leakage from payment failures, inaccurate vehicle identification and tampered tags, and calls for stronger ANPR camera coverage and tighter integration with the VAHAN registry.There is also the matter of the motorist who never sees the notice. The 72-hour window is short, and the penalty is a doubled fee and, potentially, a blacklisted tag. A vehicle owner whose registered mobile number is out of date, or who does not check SMS regularly, is the person most exposed. That is a question for the next phase as much as for the first.India’s highway toll system is changing in stages. FASTag took the cash out of the booth. MLFF now aims to take out the booth itself. Seven plazas, an expanding bid pipeline and a first set of figures show the direction of travel, but the pace is behind the original target, and a network of over 1,150 plazas will not change quickly.What the next phase has to show is whether the compliance rate improves as more motorists link their tags and plates correctly, and whether the savings the ministry projects begin to show at the plazas that have already gone live.
Article Summary: Multi-Lane Free Flow (MLFF) lets vehicles pass through toll locations without stopping. It is still a small part of a very large network, but it marks the biggest change in how India collects highway tolls since FASTag made cashless payment routine.

NEW DELHI: University Grants Commission (UGC) has issued a fresh public advisory warning students and parents against enrolling in unrecognised institutions, even as its list of fake universities has grown from 20 to 32 in three years. More strikingly, 18 of the 20 institutions flagged in March 2023 continue to figure on the latest list, despite warnings and letters seeking action from state govts.The Nov 17 advisory, issued following Supreme Court directions, has renewed questions over the effectiveness of action against institutions accused of illegally awarding degrees. SC's intervention followed reports of an alleged fake medical college operating from a farmhouse in Etah, Uttar Pradesh.In its Oct 9 order, SC directed UGC and other regulators to issue public advisories cautioning prospective students against unauthorised institutions.A comparison of UGC's March 2023 list with its Feb 2026 list showed that 90% of the originally identified institutions remain flagged. Continued inclusion, however, does not necessarily mean an institution remains operational or that no enforcement action has been taken.Delhi accounts for the largest concentration, with 12 fake universities, up from eight in 2023. All eight institutions identified in the capital three years ago remain on the list. UP has four, while six other states and UTs have two each. UGC records revealed that the commission wrote to state education authorities in April 2023 seeking action against institutions violating UGC Act, 1956. Follow-up letters were issued in July, while a Sept communication directed the institutions concerned to submit compliance reports within 15 days.In an Aug 2026 parliamentary reply, the education ministry said states had been asked to register FIRs and initiate steps to close unauthorised institutions. The latest advisory asks students to verify institutional recognition, authority to award degrees, course approvals and permission to operate online, distance or off-campus programmes before paying fees.It cautions against relying solely on advertisements, websites, brochures or social media claims, urging independent verification through official regulatory websites.
Article Summary: University Grants Commission has issued a fresh public advisory warning students and parents against enrolling in unrecognised institutions. NEW DELHI: After a gap over two years, Indian railways will run a direct cross-border passenger train. This time to Nepal, to link Lord Ram’s birthplace Ayodhya to that of Mata Sita’s in Janakpur. The move will not only connect the two cities revered by Hindus, promoting religious tourism, but also play the larger role of strengthening bilateral relations.TOI has learnt that PM Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah will virtually flag off the train on its inaugural run on Nov 23 (Monday). As per a railway ministry notification, the weekly train from Janakpur will depart every Saturday afternoon while departure from Ayodhya will be every Monday afternoon.The last cross-border trains that India operated were Maitree and Bandhan Express to Bangladesh. The services were suspended indefinitely in July-Aug 2024 following violent protests and political turmoil in the neighbouring nation. There is no sign of the operation resuming anytime soon.Earlier, India’s passenger train services to Pakistan — Samjhauta Express and Thar Express — were suspended in Aug 2019 after govt revoked J&K’s special status under Article 320 and the subsequent deterioration in bilateral relations.So, the direct train to Janakpur will be the only active cross-border link from India in the region.“This will be the first direct passenger train from India to Nepal.At present, passengers from India can travel up to Jaynagar station in Bihar by Indian Railways, then they need to undergo customs clearance and board trains run by Nepal Railways to reach Janakpur Dham and Kurtha in Nepal. However, in the case of Ayodhya Cantt-Janakpur Dham train, passengers will continue to travel in the same train after customs clearance,” said an official.The one-way journey of around 604 km will take approximately 19 hours. The train with AC2, AC3 and sleeper coaches can accommodate around 1,100 passengers. The train will stop at stations including Mankapur, Basti, Gorakhpur, Narkatiaganj, Raxaul, Sitamarhi, Shisho, Madhubani and Jaynagar. Indian passengers need to carry a valid proof such as passport, voter-id, Aadhaar or driving licence.
Article Summary: India and Nepal are preparing to inaugurate a direct train service linking Ayodhya and Janakpur. The move will not only connect the two cities revered by Hindus, promoting religious tourism, but also play the larger role of strengthening bilateral relations. PM Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah will virtually flag off the train on its inaugural run on Nov 23.

NEW DELHI: Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh on Saturday called for the existing strength and state-wise composition of the Lok Sabha to remain unchanged until India achieves the 'Viksit Bharat' goal, while questioning the Centre's approach to the proposed delimitation exercise.He also flagged the absence of consultations with political parties, saying 100 days had passed since the 2026 Monsoon Session of Parliament was adjourned sine die without being prorogued.In a post on X, Ramesh alleged that the government was yet to secure the required two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha to pass the Constitutional Amendment Bill on delimitation.He also questioned the lack of clarity on a fresh Bill, pointing out that the earlier legislation was defeated on April 17, 2026. Ramesh claimed that no fresh proposals had been discussed with political parties in a structured manner and no all-party meeting had been called, despite Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge writing four letters to the Prime Minister.Arguing that delimitation was not an immediate priority, Ramesh said the country faced more pressing economic, political, social, military and foreign policy challenges. "Far-reaching and comprehensive Delimitation can wait," he said, citing the decisions of former prime ministers Indira Gandhi and Atal Bihari Vajpayee to defer the exercise.Ramesh recalled that Indira Gandhi had postponed delimitation by 25 years in 1976, while Vajpayee extended the freeze for another 25 years in 2001, until the publication of the first Census after 2026. Describing the two leaders as "wise and nationalist PMs", he argued that the exercise could be deferred again."Under the circumstances, it is in the nation's interest to let the current Lok Sabha strength and state-wise configuration continue with one-third reservation for women implemented," Ramesh said.He proposed that the existing arrangement remain frozen until the 'Viksit Bharat' objective is achieved, arguing that the consequences of a fundamental change in delimitation could be better managed once the country's development goal becomes a reality.
Article Summary: Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh called for the existing strength and state-wise composition of the Lok Sabha to remain unchanged until India achieves the 'Viksit Bharat' goal. He also flagged the absence of consultations with political parties, saying 100 days had passed since the 2026 Monsoon Session of Parliament was adjourned.

Leh Police on Friday night removed security arrangements put in place to ensure compliance with a prohibitory order imposed on climate activist Sonam Wangchuk in Leh, officials said.The police also clarified that Wangchuk had not been placed under house arrest, cited by the PTI. He questioned how authorities could prevent someone from taking part in a peaceful protest without formally arresting them.The activist had alleged that the restrictions were imposed while he and other members of the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) were preparing to stage a sit-in protest over various demands concerning Ladakh.The proposed demonstration was also linked to concerns over the timing of the upcoming elections to the Autonomous Hill Development Councils, scheduled to be held on December 4.
Article Summary: Leh Police on Friday night removed security arrangements put in place to ensure compliance with a prohibitory order imposed on climate activist Sonam Wangchuk. Article Title: India looks beyond borders to secure critical minerals, says mines secretary
Article Text:
India looks beyond borders to secure critical minerals

NEW DELHI: India is exploring opportunities to secure critical mineral supplies through both domestic resources and overseas investments, ministry of mines secretary Keshav Chandra said, underlining the government's efforts to strengthen mineral security through policy reforms, exploration and international partnerships.Speaking at a closed-door industry interaction organised by the mines ministry and the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), Chandra outlined the government's reform agenda to improve the global competitiveness of the mining sector. According to news agency ANI, the focus areas include geological exploration, responsible mining, advanced processing, research, recycling and technology-enabled governance.Chandra also highlighted recent auction reforms, including the relaxation of minimum bidder requirements for certain minerals and the automatic issuance of Letters of Intent. Responding to industry concerns, he discussed measures already undertaken and those under consideration to address operational challenges in developing mineral blocks.He urged companies to explore the extraction of critical minerals from alternative resources, including red mud, an industrial residue generated during aluminium production.The interaction also saw the launch of a concept paper titled Enabling Overseas Investment in Critical Minerals: Policy, Financial and Institutional Framework for Securing India's Critical Mineral Supply Chains.Chandra said the paper's focus on moving from memorandums of understanding (MoUs) to actual project delivery was aligned with the ministry's efforts, including the overseas engagements of Khanij Bidesh India Ltd (KABIL). He expressed interest in examining the recommendations made in the paper.On overseas investments, the secretary emphasised the need for enabling mechanisms to improve project viability. He said the ministry would continue addressing industry concerns through policy and regulatory reforms, institutional coordination and targeted interventions.Opening the interaction, Pankaj Satija, Co-Chair of the FICCI Mining Committee and Executive Vice-President of JSW, welcomed the ministry's reforms in exploration, mineral auctions and mine operationalisation.Satija also flagged growing vulnerabilities in global supply chains arising from export controls, domestic value-addition requirements and restrictions on processing technologies. He stressed the need for diversified and resilient mineral supply chains to support India's industrial and economic security.According to FICCI, the concept paper was prepared following a mandate from the Ministry of Mines and draws on research and stakeholder consultations. It identifies barriers to overseas mineral investments and proposes solutions, including a Country-Priority Mineral Matrix and a tiered framework to prioritise projects for government support.The paper also calls for stronger institutional coordination, streamlined approvals and closer integration of overseas investments with India's domestic processing and manufacturing capabilities.
Article Summary: India is exploring opportunities to secure critical mineral supplies through both domestic resources and overseas investments. Ministry of mines secretary Keshav Chandra outlined the government's reform agenda to improve the global competitiveness of the mining sector. The focus areas include geological exploration, responsible mining, advanced processing, research, recycling and technology-enabled governance.

Article Title: Himalayan marmot droppings could help track climate change
Article Text:
(a, b, d): Alpine-steppe vegetation at Pensila Pass and Rimkhim; (c, e): Himalayan marmots in their natural habitats; (f, g): Marmot faeces, showing midden deposits and individual pellet morphology. | Credit: BSIP

BENGALURU: What can the droppings of a Himalayan marmot reveal about climate change? Quite a bit, according to a new study that has found pollen grains, fungal spores and elemental signatures preserved in the faeces of the high-altitude herbivore can provide clues to changing vegetation and environmental conditions in the higher Himalaya.Scientists from the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP), an autonomous institute under the Department of Science and Technology, explored whether marmot faeces could serve as an alternative biological archive to reconstruct environmental changes. Their findings, published in the journal PLOS One, could offer a useful tool for studying remote, arid mountain environments where conventional sources of palaeoenvironmental evidence are scarce.The Himalaya is particularly sensitive to changes in temperature, precipitation and snow cover. Such changes can affect alpine vegetation and wildlife habitats. Traditionally, scientists have relied on lake sediments, peat and soil to reconstruct past environmental conditions. The researchers sought to establish whether biological material preserved in marmot droppings could provide similar insights.The Himalayan marmot (Marmota himalayana) inhabits cold, dry alpine environments and depends on local vegetation for food and shelter. Pollen preserved in its faeces reflects the plants consumed by the animal, thereby offering a record of the surrounding alpine-steppe vegetation.The research team analysed faecal samples collected from two Himalayan regions, using pollen and fungal-spore identification, statistical methods and Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy coupled with Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (FESEM-EDS) to determine elemental composition.The analysis identified several plant groups in the marmot's diet, including Artemisia, Asteroideae, Caryophyllaceae, Poaceae, Cyperaceae and Chenopodiaceae. Researchers also examined ratios between three pollen combinations: Artemisia/Chenopodiaceae, Artemisia/Cyperaceae and Artemisia/Ephedra. These were used to interpret vegetation patterns and associated climatic conditions.The results showed that the marmot's mixed plant-based diet was dominated by groups such as Artemisia, Asteroideae, Caryophyllaceae and Chenopodiaceae, reflecting the characteristics of alpine vegetation. The researchers concluded that the Himalayan marmot could serve as an indicator species for understanding vegetation and climate changes in the higher Himalaya.The study also found that changes in marmot habitats could indicate shifts in altitude associated with changing environmental conditions. Combining pollen, fungal spores and elemental analysis could therefore provide a modern reference for future palaeoecological studies and help reconstruct past ecological changes.The findings could have implications beyond climate research. Marmots are an important prey species for snow leopards, and a better understanding of their habitat requirements could help monitor changes in the wider ecosystem and inform wildlife conservation strategies.
Article Summary: Pollen grains, fungal spores and elemental signatures preserved in the faeces of the high-altitude herbivore can provide clues to changing vegetation and environmental conditions in the higher Himalaya. The findings could offer a useful tool for studying remote, arid mountain environments where conventional sources of palaeoenvironmental evidence are scarce.

Article Title: NMC hikes appeal fee for medical colleges up to six-fold; private institutions to pay Rs 3.54 lakh
Article Text:
Medical colleges in India will face significantly higher appeal fees to challenge National Medical Commission's decisions.

NEW DELHI:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Medical colleges will now have to pay substantially more to challenge regulatory decisions of the National Medical Commission (NMC), with the regulator increasing its appeal fee from Rs 59,000 to Rs 1.77 lakh for government institutions and Rs 3.54 lakh for private and deemed universities, including GST.Under the revised fee structure, government medical colleges will have to pay Rs 1.77 lakh to appeal against decisions taken by the NMC’s Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB), Undergraduate Medical Education Board (UGMEB) and Postgraduate Medical Education Board (PGMEB). Private medical colleges and deemed universities will have to pay Rs 3.54 lakh for filing such appeals.Earlier, all institutions, irrespective of whether they were government or privately run, paid a uniform fee of Rs 59,000, including 18 per cent GST. The new structure effectively triples the fee for government colleges and increases it six-fold for private and deemed institutions.The revised charges will apply to appeals relating to the 2026-27 academic year onwards, according to a public notice issued by the NMC on Friday.The revision covers appeals filed under Sections 22(3), 28(5) and 35(5) of the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and other relevant regulations.The NMC said the existing appeal fee had been reviewed and the revised rates approved by the competent authority.The Commission has directed all medical colleges and institutions to pay the applicable revised fee while submitting appeals. It has also cautioned that appeals filed without payment of the prescribed amount are liable to be rejected.All such appeals will have to be submitted through the respective online appeal modules of the Commission.EOM
Article Summary: The National Medical Commission has increased its appeal fee from Rs 59,000 to Rs 1.77 lakh. The new fee structure effectively triples the fee for government colleges and increases it six-fold for private and deemed institutions. The revised charges will apply to appeals relating to the 2026-27 academic year.

Article Title: NMC plans to simplify rules for Indians who study medicine abroad
Article Text:
The NMC has issued the amendment as a draft notification and invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and others likely to be affected.

NEW DELHI:

Indian students who obtain medical degrees abroad may get some relief from the eligibility requirements for practising in India, with the National Medical Commission (NMC) proposing to remove a condition linked to the licence required to practise medicine in the country where they studied.Under the existing rules, foreign medical graduates must be registered with the medical regulatory body in the country where they obtained their degree. They must also have a licence to practise medicine equivalent to the one given to citizens of that country.The NMC now wants to remove the second requirement. Under the proposed change, foreign medical graduates would only need to be registered with the medical regulatory body in the country where they studied. They would no longer have to meet the separate condition of holding a licence equivalent to that issued to local citizens.The proposed change is part of an amendment to the National Medical Commission (Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate) Regulations, 2021. It seeks to modify Clause 4(b) of the regulations, which deals with the eligibility of foreign medical graduates.The NMC has issued the amendment as a draft notification and invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and others likely to be affected. Comments can be submitted within 30 days from the date the Gazette notification is made available to the public.The Commission will consider the feedback before finalising the amendment. The revised provision will come into force only after its publication in the Official Gazette.
Article Summary: Under the existing rules, foreign medical graduates must be registered with the medical regulatory body in the country where they obtained their degree. They must also have a licence to practise medicine equivalent to the one given to citizens of that country. The NMC now wants to remove the second requirement.

NEW DELHI: As India hosted the first SCO Civilization Dialogue Friday, govt downplayed Pakistan's presence at the event, saying that all SCO member-states had been invited for the inaugural talks proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi last year. The ministry of external affairs also strongly denied that India's position on the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty , which was put in abeyance after the Pahalgam terrorist attack last year, had changed."This is a multilateral event within the SCO framework, for which invitations have been extended to all members of the SCO, including Pakistan. Observers and Dialogue Partners of the SCO have also been invited to attend the dialogue, which will be inaugurated by the PM," said spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal.Pakistan's Musadik Masood Malik, federal minister for climate change and environmental coordination, is leading the country's delegation. After they became full members of the Eurasian bloc in 2017, India and Pakistan have regularly engaged at the multilateral forum, without letting bilateral differences get in the way. This is the first ministerial visit from Pakistan in over three years and also after the Pahalgam attack.Indian govt denied that it had placed any restriction on the movement of Malik or any other minister participating in the event. While there was a security issue that may not have allowed him to visit Nizamuddin, official sources said all ministers were free to travel anywhere, including to Taj Mahal and Humayun's tomb."I think all our relationships will improve. The region is in flux and the geopolitical landscape is shifting very fast. I am hopeful that we will take a broader view, looking at political and social issues as well as other areas of engagement, and push the regional agenda," said Malik, speaking on the margins of the event."Dialogue is between distinct entities. Singularity does not require dialogue; it requires a monologue. Dialogue is about diversity. India, Pakistan, Russia, China and the Central Asian states share historical connections that can be traced through archaeological excavations. This is a welcome dialogue," Malik further said.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Musadik Masood Malik, federal minister for climate change and environmental coordination, is leading the country's delegation. India and Pakistan have regularly engaged at the multilateral forum, without letting bilateral differences get in the way. This is the first ministerial visit from Pakistan in over three years and also after the Pahalgam attack.

Article Title: No China input yet on GoPro cam used during Pahalgam attack: NIA
Article Text:
NIA says China is yet to respond to India's request for information on the GoPro camera recovered from the terrorists involved in the 2025 Pahalgam attack.

NEW DELHI: NIA director general Rakesh Aggarwal Thursday said China is yet to respond to the agency's request seeking details of the supply chain that landed a US-manufactured GoPro camera, shipped to a Chinese commercial distributor, in the hands of Pakistani terrorists behind the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam attack, reports Bharti Jain.The GoPro camera was worn by the terrorists as they gunned down 26 people, including 25 tourists, in front of their families in Pahalgam. However, NIA sources said no footage was recovered from the camera, seized from the hideout of the terrorists in Dachigam after they were neutralised in July 2025.Regarding allegations by US national Mathew VanDyke - arrested in March for illegally using India as a transit point to Myanmar where he offered arms training to ultras - that he was mistreated during custody in Tihar jail, Aggarwal said VanDyke never raised this allegation during his appearance in the court here some 6-7 times.
Article Summary: NIA says China is yet to respond to India's request for information on the GoPro camera recovered from the terrorists involved in the 2025 Pahalgam attack. GoPro camera was worn by the terrorists as they gunned down 26 people, including 25 tourists, in front of their families.
